svg.title: Stories of the past and future — the local-time corpus
svg.desc: Each entry is a work plotted at its publication date and how far its setting sits from that date: 104 entries, 11 obsolete, 9 still possible, 45 former period pieces, 39 recognisable past settings. Chart form after xkcd #1491.

g.aria-label: the cone: settings the reader's present has overtaken
g.text: and older than this, the future is already past

g.title: Epic of Gilgamesh — 2100 BCE, set ~2600 BCE; former period piece — published closer to its setting than to you
g.desc: Enmebaragesi, a historically attested *Epic of Gilgamesh* character, is thought to have lived around 2600 BCE

g.title: The Iliad — 700 BCE, set 1260–1240 BCE; former period piece — published closer to its setting than to you
Book of Genesis — 400 BCE, set 3761 BCE; set in the past, and recognisably so
g.desc: The *Anno Mundi* epoch, the product of scriptural calculations by Maimonides, places the Genesis date of the creation of the world at October 7, 3761 BCE in the proleptic Julian calendar

g.title: History of the Peloponnesian War — 400 BCE, set 431–411 BCE; former period piece — published closer to its setting than to you
Gospels — 65, set 7–2 BCE – 30–33 CE; former period piece — published closer to its setting than to you
g.desc: Setting dates are those of Jesus' estimated lifetime. Writing dates are as follows: Mark 65–73 CE; Matthew 70–100 CE; Luke 80–100 CE; John 90–110 CE. Randall's difference calculation seems to be based on the date of Jesus' death, as the majority of the Gospels' events takes place during the three years prior to Jesus's death.

g.title: Golf in the Year 2000 — 1892, set 2000; obsolete — its future has arrived
The Time Machine — 1895, set 802,701– 1 billion; still possible
g.desc: Note that Randall has included only part of the book; which includes scenes all the way from the time of writing to the death of the last life on Earth. The novel itself identifies the latest part as being "more than thirty million years" in the future, based on the theories of the Sun's lifespan at the time.

Star Wars (IV – VI) — 1977, set "A long time ago"; set in the past, and recognisably so
g.desc: It's not clear why Randall has chosen 1 billion years here. Wookieepedia puts the age of the *Star Wars* galaxy at ~13 billion years, and our Universe is only 13.8 billion years old, and the oldest known galaxy took 380 million years to form... So it would seem *Star Wars* should be no farther than 400 million years in the past, give or take.
